speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I see you are a newborn presenting with respiratory distress; to begin our assessment, how old are you in days or weeks, and are you breathing normally or are you using extra muscles to breathe?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, born after the 32nd gestational week. The baby was born via cesarean delivery. The mother had gestational diabetes but was otherwise healthy with no other pregnancy-related diseases.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the history. Given your premature birth (post-32 weeks) and cesarean delivery, are you currently experiencing grunting, nasal flaring, or noticeable retractions when your baby breathes?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Respiratory distress. I also have Tachypnea, Subcostal and intercostal retractions, Nasal flaring, Cyanosis.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS).

The clinical picture of a 32-week premature infant presenting with tachypnea, grunting (implied by distress), nasal flaring, cyanosis, and significant retractions (subcostal and intercostal) is classic for alveolar collapse due to surfactant deficiency. I am requesting an immediate Chest X-Ray to confirm the ground-glass appearance and air bronchograms typical of RDS.
